turns_text: [SEG0001] person_1 (NURSE): Howzit, I'm Sister Dlamini. I'll grab your vitals before the doctor calls you, so have a seat.
[SEG0002] person_2 (PATIENT): Eish, okay. Is this going to take long? My bakkie's on a meter outside and I don't want a ticket.
[SEG0003] person_3 (FAMILY_MEMBER): The meter can wait, Sipho. Sorry, sister, he's been wound up since we left Germiston.

[SEG0004] person_1 (NURSE): Shame, the N1 was hectic, I know. First reading is one forty-two over ninety... ag, no, he'd just sat, so let me repeat it. One thirty-eight over eighty-six, pulse seventy-eight, oxygen ninety-eight percent.
[SEG0005] person_2 (PATIENT): Is one thirty-eight bad? Should I worry? My dad's pressure was always high and that scares me.
[SEG0006] person_1 (NURSE): It's not sky-high, the doctor will explain it. Weight is eighty-one kilograms. He'll be with you just now.
[SEG0007] person_4 (DOCTOR): Morning, I'm Dr Naidoo. I've got sister's numbers here. What brings you in?

[SEG0008] person_3 (FAMILY_MEMBER): He didn't really want to come, doctor. We live together in Germiston, and since he got retrenched he's not sleeping, he's got no get-up-and-go, and he's lost interest in everything. I'm Naledi, his wife.
[SEG0009] person_2 (PATIENT): I'm fine. Seriously, she's overreacting. I just need one decent night and I'll be sharp.
[SEG0010] person_4 (DOCTOR): I'll hear you both, Sipho, but I need your version as well. Naledi, how long has this actually been going?
[SEG0011] person_3 (FAMILY_MEMBER): The retrenchment from the logistics depot was five months ago. The not-sleeping started with that. He lies awake till two, sometimes three.
[SEG0012] person_2 (PATIENT): It hasn't been five months. The sleep thing is more like two months. Before that I was angry about the job, not awake all night.
[SEG0013] person_4 (DOCTOR): So two months from you, about five from your wife. I'll park it as somewhere in that range rather than force a date.
[SEG0014] person_2 (PATIENT): Is bad sleep dangerous, though? Can it damage your heart? I read something ugly on my phone last night.
[SEG0015] person_4 (DOCTOR): A short run of bad nights won't wreck a heart on its own. Months of it wears you out, which is why we're here. What do the nights actually look like?

[SEG0016] person_2 (PATIENT): I'm in bed around eleven, then my brain goes on about work, the bond, money. I might drift off near four. Then the neighbour's dog gets me at half past five and that's me done.
[SEG0017] person_3 (FAMILY_MEMBER): And in the daytime he's a flat battery. Soccer can be on and he doesn't even shout at the TV, which is not my husband.
[SEG0018] person_2 (PATIENT): Ja, well, the PSL isn't lekker this season. But... okay. I don't feel like five-a-side anymore, I used to go Tuesdays, and now I just think, what's the point.
[SEG0019] person_4 (DOCTOR): Is that what's-the-point only about soccer, or about more of the day?

[SEG0020] person_2 (PATIENT): More of the day, if I'm honest. I don't phone my mates, and the applications sit half finished. I'm not crying or anything. I just feel heavy, low energy, and nothing's interesting.
[SEG0021] person_3 (FAMILY_MEMBER): He picks at supper too. I dish up at home and he says he's not hungry, and his jeans are looser, I swear.
[SEG0022] person_2 (PATIENT): I'm eating, just not big plates, don't make it a whole thing. Is losing weight a sign of cancer? My uncle had stomach cancer and now I'm spiralling.
[SEG0023] person_4 (DOCTOR): Smaller plates and a cancer worry are different things, and nothing here screams cancer, so I'm not chasing that today. Any tummy pain, vomiting, or blood in the stool?
[SEG0024] person_2 (PATIENT): No. No pain, no vomiting, nothing like blood. Um, should I still be scared, though?
[SEG0025] person_4 (DOCTOR): Not on what you've told me. And the low energy, is that every day?
[SEG0026] person_2 (PATIENT): Pretty much every day, the same stretch as the sleep. Mornings are the worst. By evening I can manage a bit, like make tea or answer a text.
[SEG0027] person_3 (FAMILY_MEMBER): And the interest, doctor. He loved a braai, and if my brother comes past now Sipho just disappears to the bedroom.
[SEG0028] person_2 (PATIENT): Crowds tire me out. It's not that I hate them, I just can't be bothered. Is that depression, be straight with me, am I going mad?

[SEG0029] person_4 (DOCTOR): You're not going mad. Thinking out loud, low interest, poor sleep and low energy after losing a job can be a depressive episode, or it can be an adjustment to the retrenchment. I can't cleanly split those two today.
[SEG0030] person_2 (PATIENT): So which one is it? Does depression stay forever? Will I lose my licence? I still drive the bakkie for piece jobs.

[SEG0031] person_4 (DOCTOR): Neither one is a life sentence, and nothing we discuss today stops you driving. I do need to ask something direct, and I'll do it gently. Have you had any thoughts of hurting yourself, or that you'd be better off not being here?
[SEG0032] person_2 (PATIENT): No. Definitely not. I've never thought of harming myself, I want to be around for Naledi, I'm just stuck.
[SEG0033] person_3 (FAMILY_MEMBER): He's told me the same thing. He gets gloomy, not that kind of gloomy. I do watch him, though.

[SEG0034] person_4 (DOCTOR): Thank you, both of you, that's plain and it helps. If that ever changes, don't wait for an appointment, come in or go to casualty. Naledi, you can bring him if you're worried.
[SEG0035] person_2 (PATIENT): Which casualty, though? After hours, is there a number I should save? I get anxious at night just thinking about this.
[SEG0036] person_4 (DOCTOR): Any emergency unit near you is fine, state or private. If you feel unsafe you go, you don't sit in a phone queue. We'll put that line on your summary.
[SEG0037] person_3 (FAMILY_MEMBER): Queues, shame. We sat ages at that robot by the stadium because the cricket was on. The Proteas were playing and the traffic just died.
[SEG0038] person_2 (PATIENT): Did you catch the last over? I only had the radio in the bakkie. I thought they were finished, and then that catch on the boundary, eish.
[SEG0039] person_4 (DOCTOR): It was on in the tearoom. I thought they were gone once they needed more than ten an over, and then that six over cover. Proper game, that.
[SEG0040] person_3 (FAMILY_MEMBER): My dad would've been yelling at the screen. He always said a day-night in Joburg beats any movie. The weather was perfect too, not too hot, just a breeze.
[SEG0041] person_2 (PATIENT): Ja, that wind off the mine dumps. We were at my cousin's braai when it blew like that and the coals took forever. Anyway, that's not important, sorry.
[SEG0042] person_4 (DOCTOR): Sounds lekker, anyway. Let me drag us back before we start picking a squad. What medicines are you actually swallowing these days?
[SEG0043] person_2 (PATIENT): Pharmapress for the pressure, most mornings, five milligrams. And the purple one for the burn, Nexium.

[SEG0044] person_3 (FAMILY_MEMBER): The Pharmapress isn't five, Sipho. The box at home is ten milligrams, you mix that up every time. And you skip it whenever you say you feel fine, though it's meant to be every morning.

[SEG0045] person_4 (DOCTOR): Right, so the script is once a day for your blood pressure, the hypertension we already know about, but days get missed and I won't guess between five and ten milligrams. Bring the box next time.
[SEG0046] person_2 (PATIENT): The Nexium is forty milligrams... no, sorry, twenty milligrams, one in the morning. I've been on it for years for the reflux.
[SEG0047] person_3 (FAMILY_MEMBER): He also got a small yellow tablet at Clicks for energy, last month. Tiny yellow thing. He can't tell me the name, and I can't either.

[SEG0048] person_2 (PATIENT): Ja, some mornings I take it. The lady said it was for energy, and I don't even know if it's a vitamin. Is it dangerous with the pressure pill, and should I stop it today?
[SEG0049] person_4 (DOCTOR): I can't judge a tablet with no name, so don't add any more, and I won't tell you to stop it or mix it until I see the container. Bring that with the Pharmapress box.

[SEG0050] person_2 (PATIENT): I also tried sleeping tablets, the blue ones, Stilnox. I told my brother five milligrams but that was wrong, the packet was ten milligrams. I took them about a week and stopped, they made me feel drunk in the morning.
[SEG0051] person_4 (DOCTOR): So you stopped after about a week of ten milligrams, because of that hungover feeling. When did you actually stop?
[SEG0052] person_2 (PATIENT): Sometime last month? Or maybe the month before. I honestly can't pin the date.
[SEG0053] person_3 (FAMILY_MEMBER): It was before my sister's wedding, so I reckon longer than a month. I couldn't give you the day either.
[SEG0054] person_4 (DOCTOR): Then we won't invent a date. The reflux you've had for years can stay on the Nexium as it is. Any Grandpa, any Allergex, anything from the spaza?

[SEG0055] person_2 (PATIENT): Grandpa powders if I get a headache, not often, and no Allergex. I don't smoke, I never have. Beers, though, most nights, three or four, since the retrenchment. Is that too much, and will beer fight with whatever you give me?

[SEG0056] person_4 (DOCTOR): Three or four most nights is more than I want while your mood is down, and it chops up your sleep. I'm not banning you, I'm asking you to cut back so it's not most nights. We'll get to a tablet in a minute, and yes, alcohol matters with it.
[SEG0057] person_2 (PATIENT): Cut back to what, exactly? Two beers, weekends only? If you don't give me a number I'll stress the whole time.
[SEG0058] person_4 (DOCTOR): Aim for a couple of nights a week, and fewer than three or four when you do drink. There's no magic number. Any medicine that doesn't agree with you, any allergy?
[SEG0059] person_2 (PATIENT): No. No allergies. Nothing at all.
[SEG0060] person_3 (FAMILY_MEMBER): That's not the whole story. Amoxicillin, those red and grey capsules, years back, he came out in a rash. The clinic told him to stop it.
[SEG0061] person_2 (PATIENT): That wasn't an allergy. I felt nauseous and they panicked, there was no rash. I don't have allergies.

[SEG0062] person_4 (DOCTOR): I won't force the two of you to agree. I'll note a possible amoxicillin rash from Naledi, which you don't accept, and we'll simply avoid amoxicillin until it's clearer. There's no test for that today.
[SEG0063] person_2 (PATIENT): So if I get a sinus thing I can't have that one? What do I take instead? And will this maybe-rash mess with my medical aid?
[SEG0064] person_4 (DOCTOR): There are plenty of other antibiotics, and a medical aid won't blacklist you over a maybe. Park that worry for now.

[SEG0065] person_4 (DOCTOR): Hop on the bed for a second. Lungs are clear, heart sounds are normal, and there's no swelling at the ankles. You look tired, and your face goes a bit flat when we talk about the job, but you're following me fine.
[SEG0066] person_2 (PATIENT): A flat face, is that a stroke? My cheek feels normal. Please check again, I'm not joking.
[SEG0067] person_4 (DOCTOR): Not a stroke. Both sides of your face move the same, your grip is equal, and your speech is clear. I'm describing your mood, not a nerve problem.

[SEG0068] person_3 (FAMILY_MEMBER): His mother was on antidepressants for years, for depression, and he's always been scared he'll end up the same. She passed on, but that was long before this job business.
[SEG0069] person_2 (PATIENT): I don't want her tablets. I think she was on Prozac. If you give me that, I'll feel labelled for life, won't I?

[SEG0070] person_4 (DOCTOR): I wasn't going to copy her script. If we medicate later, the one I usually reach for in this picture is sertraline, fifty milligrams in the morning, not Prozac. We are not starting anything today.

[SEG0071] person_2 (PATIENT): Why not today? If this is depression, isn't waiting dangerous? What about side effects, will I get fat, or sleep even worse, or get addicted? I need all of that before I even consider a tablet.

[SEG0072] person_4 (DOCTOR): Sertraline isn't addictive the way Stilnox can be. Early on, people can get nausea or feel a bit restless, sleep can swing either way, and weight gain isn't the rule. Starting today feels rushed, with the allergy story still muddy and this being our first sit-down. We'll use the next few weeks for sleep habits and less beer, and if you're still this flat then, we start the sertraline.

[SEG0073] person_2 (PATIENT): A few weeks is so vague, what if I crash before that? My cousin says you must always check the thyroid. Are you doing bloods today, and I haven't eaten, does that ruin them?

[SEG0074] person_4 (DOCTOR): Not today. If the sleep and the mood haven't shifted by the time I see you again, then I'll book a thyroid test and a full blood count. Fasting isn't needed for those, and we're not drawing them now.
[SEG0075] person_2 (PATIENT): So when do I actually come back? And at two in the morning, when I'm staring at the ceiling, what do I do? Give me steps, otherwise I'll google and panic.

[SEG0076] person_4 (DOCTOR): Come back in three weeks, and I'll have reception slot it. Keep the same wake-up time, no phone in the bed, and if you're still awake after about twenty minutes, get up into a low light and don't use beer to knock yourself out. If any thought of harming yourself shows up, it's casualty, don't wait out the three weeks. Bring the Pharmapress box and that yellow tablet.
[SEG0077] person_2 (PATIENT): Three weeks, okay. If the yellow thing is just a vitamin, can it sit in the cupboard till then? And do I still take the Nexium tomorrow morning?

[SEG0078] person_4 (DOCTOR): Leave the yellow one in the cupboard until I've seen the container. Carry on with the Nexium tomorrow as usual, and with the Pharmapress on the days you already take it. We'll sort that dose when the box is in front of me.

spec.situation: Adult with poor sleep, low energy and loss of interest for months after a job loss or bereavement; partner or parent speaks for them; patient says 'I'm fine' then partly opens up; denies thoughts of self-harm clearly (doctor asks gently); medication discussed but not started today.
features: tangent_small_talk: a long tangent or small talk (traffic, cricket, the weather, a grandchild) that holds NO clinical content; nothing from it is extracted.
self_correction: a speaker states a number, drug name or duration and then corrects it in the same turn or later ('seventy-five... no, hundred and fifty'). The label holds only the corrected value.

colloquial_drug_names: medicines referred to by colour, purpose or brand ('the water tablet', 'Crocin', 'my sugar tablets', 'the purple inhaler'); the name is recorded as said, the normalized name only if it is clear.

spoken_numbers: doses, vitals and durations are spoken as words or sloppy speech ('a hundred and two point five', 'one-forty over ninety', 'five-ish years', 'twenty milligram'); the label writes them normally (102.5, 140/90, 20 mg) and does not turn vague ones into exact ones.

omissions.text: Initial blood pressure reading was 142/90 mmHg before repeat measurement.
Poor sleep details not recorded: he goes to bed around 11 pm, may only drift off near 4 am, and is woken by the neighbour's dog at about 5:30 am.
Depressive symptom detail not recorded: he feels 'heavy' and has stopped phoning friends, with job applications left half finished.
Loss of appetite/weight change history is disputed: wife says he is not hungry and his jeans are looser, but patient says he is still eating, just smaller portions.
Negative finding not recorded: the patient denied ever having thoughts of harming himself and said he wanted to be around for Naledi.
Pharmapress adherence detail not fully recorded: he takes it 'most mornings' and skips it when he feels fine, although it is meant to be every morning.
The doctor specifically advised not to add any more of the unnamed yellow tablet until the container is reviewed; he did not tell him to continue taking it.
Stilnox adverse effect not recorded: 10 mg made him feel 'drunk'/'hungover' in the morning, leading him to stop it after about a week.
Alcohol counselling detail not recorded: the doctor said beer is likely worsening his sleep as well as being too much while his mood is low.

Allergy history is recorded incompletely: patient denied allergies and said the amoxicillin episode was nausea without rash, while wife reported a rash; doctor documented it only as a possible amoxicillin rash to avoid for now.
Examination finding not recorded: the doctor said the patient was 'following me fine' during the mental state/general assessment.
Doctor advised there is no test for the possible amoxicillin allergy today.

Medication plan detail not fully recorded: the doctor said sertraline 50 mg in the morning is the medicine he would usually use in this situation, but specifically said they are not starting anything today because it feels rushed on a first visit and the allergy history is still unclear.
Investigation plan detail not recorded: fasting is not required for the possible future thyroid test and full blood count.
Safety-net detail not recorded: for after-hours deterioration or if he feels unsafe, the doctor said any nearby state or private emergency unit is fine and not to wait in a phone queue.
